blocks.content: Deadlock does not happen because of any single mistake. It happens only when four separate conditions are all true for the same set of processes at the same moment: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. This chapter gives each of those four conditions its own full explanation, its own concrete example, and its own diagram, so you can recognize every one of them the instant you see it in real code.

These four conditions, first formalized by E. G. Coffman and colleagues in 1971, are often called the Coffman conditions. They are not four independent causes of deadlock. They are four requirements that must all be satisfied together, like four separate locks on a single door that only opens when every one of them clicks into place at once.

The reason this topic exists on its own, separate from the lighter introduction in Deadlock Basics, is that these four conditions are the single most important idea in the entire Deadlocks module. Every prevention strategy, every avoidance algorithm, and every detection mechanism you will study later is, at its core, a different way of reacting to this same checklist of four.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408658667-724328729.png
1. Why All Four Conditions Must Hold At Once
blocks.text: 1. Why All Four Conditions Must Hold At Once

blocks.content: A deadlock can only occur if mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait are all present simultaneously in the same set of processes and resources. If a system satisfies three of the four conditions but somehow rules out the fourth, deadlock among those processes is not just unlikely, it is mathematically impossible.

This is the single most useful fact in the whole topic of deadlocks. It means you do not need to eliminate all four conditions to make a system safe from deadlock. You only need to make sure at least one of them can never happen, anywhere in that particular combination of resources and processes, and the rest of the checklist becomes irrelevant.

blocks.title: In One Sentence
blocks.content: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait must all be true at the same time for deadlock to occur; break even one of them and deadlock becomes structurally impossible.
2. Condition One: Mutual Exclusion

Mutual exclusion, in the context of deadlock, means that at least one of the resources involved must be held in a non shareable way: only one process or thread can use it at a time, and any other process that wants it must simply wait. If every resource in a system could be shared freely by any number of processes at once, nothing would ever need to wait for anything, and deadlock could never form in the first place.

The classic concrete example is a printer. A printer can only physically print one document at a time, so the operating system grants exclusive access to whichever process currently owns the active print job. Every other process that tries to print while that job is running is simply queued and made to wait, because sharing the printer mid document is not physically possible.

Not every resource behaves this way. A read only file can usually be opened by many processes at once without any conflict, so it does not contribute to mutual exclusion at all. It is specifically the non shareable resources, such as a printer, a write lock, or a single database connection, that create this condition.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408658668-364120258.png
3. Condition Two: Hold and Wait

Hold and wait describes a process that is already holding at least one resource while it simultaneously asks for another resource that it does not yet have. The process does not give up what it already holds just because its new request cannot be satisfied immediately; it keeps its grip on the first resource and simply blocks, waiting for the second one to become available.

Picture a process that first acquires a lock on a configuration file so it can safely read settings from it. While that file lock is still held, the same process then tries to acquire a connection from a database connection pool. If the pool happens to be exhausted, the process now sits there waiting for a connection, all the while continuing to hold the file lock that some other process might urgently need.

This pattern is extremely common in real backend systems, which is exactly why it matters so much. Any code path that grabs one resource and only then reaches out for a second one, without releasing the first, satisfies hold and wait the moment that second request has to block.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408658668-155338498.png

blocks.title: Why This Shows Up So Often
blocks.content: Hold and wait is rarely intentional. It usually appears simply because a function acquires resources in the natural order the code happens to need them, without anyone designing that order on purpose.
4. Condition Three: No Preemption

No preemption means that a resource cannot be forcibly taken away from the process currently holding it. The only way that resource becomes free again is if the process holding it chooses, on its own, to release it, usually once it has finished whatever it was doing with that resource.

This is different from how the operating system treats the CPU itself. A scheduler can absolutely preempt a running process off the CPU and hand that time slice to someone else; that is a normal and expected part of scheduling. A lock, a file handle, or a database row lock does not work that way. The operating system has no general mechanism to reach into a process mid update and yank a lock back out from under it, because doing so could leave shared data in a half updated, corrupted state.

Concretely, imagine a process is in the middle of updating a shared record and is holding the lock that protects it. Even if that process is stuck waiting on something else and making no progress at all, the operating system cannot simply grab that lock back and hand it to a different process. It has to wait, exactly like everyone else, for the holder to release it voluntarily.
A CPU time slice can be taken away without asking. A held lock cannot.

blocks.title: Two Different Meanings of Preemption
blocks.content: Do not confuse preemption in CPU scheduling, which is normal and constant, with preemption of a held resource like a lock, which the operating system deliberately does not do, because it would break correctness.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408658668-638160330.png
5. Condition Four: Circular Wait

Circular wait means there exists a closed chain of two or more processes, where each process in the chain is waiting for a resource that is held by the very next process in that same chain, and the last process in the chain is waiting for a resource held by the first one. The chain forms a complete loop with no exit anywhere along it.

The smallest and most common version of this is the classic two thread, two lock scenario. Thread A acquires Lock1 and then requests Lock2. Thread B acquires Lock2 and then requests Lock1. If both threads manage to grab their first lock before either one reaches its second request, Thread A ends up waiting on Thread B, and Thread B ends up waiting on Thread A, at the very same time. That closed loop is circular wait in its purest form.

Circular wait is usually the condition that finally triggers the deadlock, even though the other three conditions were quietly already in place. Mutual exclusion made the locks non shareable, hold and wait let each thread keep its first lock while asking for the second, and no preemption meant neither lock could be taken back by force. Circular wait is simply what happens when the timing lines up so those two requests point directly at each other.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408658668-747033028.png

blocks.content: 7. Mapping The Conditions Onto The Classic Two Thread Two Lock Example
blocks.text: 7. Mapping The Conditions Onto The Classic Two Thread Two Lock Example

blocks.content: The two thread, two lock scenario from earlier is small enough to hold entirely in your head, which makes it the perfect example to map all four conditions onto explicitly. Every one of the four conditions is present in that scenario, and each one has a precise, identifiable spot in the code.

Walking through it condition by condition turns the abstraction into something concrete. Once you can point at exactly which line, or which lock, demonstrates each condition, you have genuinely understood the Coffman conditions rather than just memorized their names.

blocks.content: 8. Why This Is The Master Key To The Rest Of The Module
blocks.text: 8. Why This Is The Master Key To The Rest Of The Module

blocks.content: Every strategy covered later in the dedicated Deadlocks module is, underneath its own name and algorithm, a different stance toward these same four conditions. Understanding the four conditions deeply is what makes every later topic in this module make sense on first read, instead of feeling like a disconnected new idea.

Prevention works by structurally guaranteeing that at least one condition can never hold in a given system, for example by numbering all resources and forcing every process to request them in increasing order, which rules out circular wait entirely. Avoidance takes a softer approach: all four conditions remain possible in principle, but the operating system carefully checks each resource request in advance and refuses any request that could ever lead to all four aligning at once.

Detection and recovery takes the most relaxed stance of all. It allows all four conditions to exist and does nothing to stop them from aligning; instead it periodically checks whether a deadlock has actually formed, and if one has, it recovers after the fact, usually by forcibly terminating or rolling back one of the deadlocked processes.

{"headers":["Strategy","How It Relates To The Four Conditions"],"rows":[["Prevention","Structurally guarantees that one specific condition can never occur anywhere in the system."],["Avoidance","Lets all four conditions remain possible, but rejects any resource request that could make them all align."],["Detection and Recovery","Allows the four conditions to align and deadlock to actually happen, then finds and fixes it afterward."]]}

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes And The Interview Angle
blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes And The Interview Angle

blocks.content: Two misunderstandings come up again and again once learners first meet the four conditions, and both are worth clearing up explicitly before moving on to prevention and avoidance.

["Thinking that any single one of the four conditions, on its own, is enough to cause a deadlock. In reality all four must be true at once for the same set of processes; mutual exclusion by itself, for example, is simply normal, safe resource locking.","Forgetting that breaking even one condition, anywhere in a particular system, is enough to make deadlock structurally impossible there, even if the other three conditions are still technically present."]
items: Thinking that any single one of the four conditions, on its own, is enough to cause a deadlock. In reality all four must be true at once for the same set of processes; mutual exclusion by itself, for example, is simply normal, safe resource locking.

Forgetting that breaking even one condition, anywhere in a particular system, is enough to make deadlock structurally impossible there, even if the other three conditions are still technically present.

blocks.title: The Interview Angle
blocks.content: Being able to name all four conditions from memory, along with a quick concrete example for each, is one of the most frequently asked operating systems interview questions there is. If you can explain mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait using the printer, the file lock and database connection, the voluntarily released lock, and the two thread two lock example from this chapter, you are fully ready for that question.
